subjects.displayTitle: One light, many histories: exploring the unity of religion
subjects.introduction: What might it mean to affirm the unity of religion while taking religious differences seriously? These passages begin with the demand to show love through deeds, then explore a shared divine source, the education of humanity, and laws responsive to changing circumstances. Their images of sunlight, rivers, branches, and recurring spring invite us to look for continuity without overlooking historical development. They also ask a practical question: does religion produce fellowship, justice, and mutual assistance, or become a cause of estrangement? Accounts of shared gatherings and respectful visits give that question a human setting. Connected subjects on changing and unchanging teachings, progressive revelation, and the station of each Manifestation invite closer study of unity and distinction. The Qur’an’s affirmation of earlier prophets and Peter’s recognition of divine acceptance across nations offer comparative perspectives. Together these readings encourage inquiry into how fidelity to a tradition might deepen recognition of others.
subjects.arc: Open with love expressed through deeds and reverence for other Messengers; examine the purpose and common foundation of religion; distinguish enduring principles from changing laws; explore images of continuity and renewal; read actual encounters across communities; close with practical fellowship and further inquiry.

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 2:136 · Acknowledging earlier revelation
references.note: The verse professes faith in revelation given to Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and other prophets, refusing division among them within its affirmation of submission to God. Compare this confession with the compilation’s calls to honor earlier Messengers and apply consistent standards of recognition.

references.label: 2 · Acts 10:34–35 · Divine acceptance across nations
references.note: Peter declares that divine acceptance is not restricted by national belonging, connecting it with reverence and righteous conduct. Read this alongside the compilation’s rejection of prejudice and its practical fellowship. Consider the passage within its Christian setting without assuming that it makes every claim found in the Bahá’í account of religious unity.

subjects.displayTitle: Learning across the ages: exploring progressive revelation
subjects.introduction: How can a teaching remain faithful to its purpose while taking a new form? These passages approach religious history through the growing capacities and changing needs of humanity. A child receives nourishment by degrees; a physician changes a remedy; spring renews life without repeating every detail of an earlier season. Such images lead into the Bahá’í understanding of successive Manifestations whose common divine source does not erase the distinct tasks of their missions. The readings also examine a recurring difficulty: love for an earlier revelation can become a barrier to recognizing renewal. Neighboring subjects on enduring and changing teachings, spiritual springtime, and future revelation extend that inquiry. Jesus’ words about what his disciples could yet bear, and his images of new cloth and wine, provide comparative readings in their Gospel settings. This compilation invites reflection on how reverence, patient learning, and openness to further guidance can grow together.
subjects.arc: Begin with capacity, healing and living growth; distinguish continuity of purpose from changing laws; follow images of education, seasons and sunlight; examine recognition and prophetic succession; explore the Báb’s account of unending revelation; close with humility about finality and the gradual application of teachings.

subjects.displayTitle: Receiving and reflecting light: the Manifestation as sun
subjects.introduction: Sunlight makes things visible, nourishes growth, and reaches beyond the boundaries people draw. These passages use that familiar experience to explore the Manifestation of God as a source of spiritual life, knowledge, and moral renewal. The image also raises questions: why does one light appear differently in different mirrors, and why might someone cling to a former horizon while missing a new dawn? The readings move between the unity of the divine Messengers, the varying capacities of their recipients, and the practical work of becoming a source of kindness and illumination for others. They also acknowledge the limits of imagery before a reality beyond human comprehension. Connected subjects on the divine educator, physician, mirror, and gardener offer further ways to examine these relationships. The Qur’an’s parable of light and Jesus’ declaration in John provide comparative perspectives, inviting attention to how spiritual illumination becomes understanding, growth, and action.

questions: What does the image of the sun reveal about spiritual education that the images of teacher, physician, or gardener bring out differently?
How do the passages distinguish the source of light from its reflections? What might receiving and reflecting light mean in an ordinary relationship?
What is involved in recognizing the same light from a new horizon? How can attachment, inherited assumptions, or reliance on others affect that recognition?
How do the texts handle the apparent rising and setting of a light described as enduring? What does their use of analogy help explain, and what remains beyond it?
How do the Qur’anic parable and the passage from John connect illumination with guidance and life? What differences in their language invite closer study?
Which passages most clearly connect illumination with conduct, mutual service, or truthful speech? How might you explore that connection in practice?

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 24:35 · The parable of light
references.note: This verse develops an image of light through a niche, lamp, glass, and blessed tree, and connects it with divine guidance. Compare the parallel translations with the passage addressed to Misbah in this compilation. How do several images work together, and why might a text explicitly speak through similitudes?

references.label: 2 · John 8:12 · The light of life
references.note: Jesus describes himself as the light of the world and connects following him with the light of life. Read this verse alongside the compilation’s account of Christ’s perfections and the education of hearts. Consider how the language moves from recognizing a light to following it in one’s life.
